title: Sansara

teacherSummary.text: Over many years Siddhartha grows wealthy, gambles, drinks, and becomes greedy and weary—like the childlike people. Kamala tells him she wishes to learn about Gotama. After a dream of Kamala's songbird lying dead in its golden cage, Siddhartha feels disgust at his life and leaves the city without a word. Kamala, pregnant with his child, frees her bird.

items.text: Which line shows how Siddhartha used to look down on the childlike people? Read it to us.
items.lookFor: The line on watching them with “some mocking disdain”
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: The disdain line: “always he had watched them with some mockery, some mocking disdain, with the same disdain which a Samana constantly feels for the people of the world” (Sansara, paragraph 4). The repeated “disdain” shows how far above them he once felt.

items.text: Why does the dream about the songbird shake Siddhartha so deeply?
items.lookFor: The dead bird feels like his own worth thrown away
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: When he throws the dead bird out, “his heart hurt, as if he had thrown away from himself all value and everything good by throwing out this dead bird” (Sansara, paragraph 10). The mute bird mirrors the inner voice that has gone silent in him.

items.text: What does Kamala do when she hears that Siddhartha has disappeared?
items.lookFor: She sets free the rare singing bird from its golden cage
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “She opened the door of the cage, took the bird out and let it fly.” (Sansara, paragraph 17)

items.text: What does Siddhartha do in his mind as he sits under the tree after the dream?
items.lookFor: He goes back over the whole path of his life from his first memories
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “By and by, he gathered his thoughts, and in his mind, he once again went the entire path of his life, starting with the first days he could remember.” (Sansara, paragraph 12)

items.text: What is Sansara?
items.lookFor: The cycle of suffering and rebirth
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: The cycle of desire, suffering and rebirth; here Siddhartha names it as an endless children’s game: “The name of this game was Sansara, a game for children” (Sansara, paragraph 12).

items.text: Retell the three most important events of “Sansara” in order, in one sentence each.
items.lookFor: Over many years Siddhartha grows wealthy, gambles, drinks, and becomes greedy and weary—like the childlike people. Kamala tells him she wishes to learn about Gotama. After a dream of Kamala's songbird lying dead in its golden cage, Siddhartha feels disgust at his life and leaves the city without a word. Kamala, pregnant with his child, frees her bird.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Over the years Siddhartha sinks into wealth, gambling and weariness (Sansara, paragraphs 2–7); he dreams of Kamala’s dead songbird and feels his life is worthless (paragraphs 10–11); he leaves his garden and the city for good, and Kamala frees her bird (paragraphs 15–17).

items.text: Which characters appear or are mentioned in “Sansara”? Name two and one thing each says or does.
items.lookFor: Names and actions taken from the chapter; check against the teacher summary.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Two of: Kamala, who speaks of the Buddha with sadness and frees her bird (paragraphs 8, 17); Kamaswami, whose business Siddhartha pursues more pettily (paragraph 7); Gotama, Govinda and his father, whom he remembers under the mango tree (paragraph 14).

items.text: Where and when does “Sansara” take place? Point to the line that tells you.
items.lookFor: A place/time detail quoted from the chapter.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: In the city, his pleasure-garden and Kamala’s grove, over many years: “Years passed by; surrounded by the good life, Siddhartha hardly felt them fading away.” (Sansara, paragraph 2)

items.text: Reread: “Just slowly and imperceptibly, as the harvest seasons and rainy seasons passed by, his mockery had become more tired, his superiority had become more quiet.” What does “imperceptibly” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?
items.lookFor: imperceptibly: so gradually that it could not be noticed.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Imperceptibly” here means: so gradually that it could not be noticed. In Sansara, paragraph 4, over the years Siddhartha changes so slowly that he does not notice his mockery and pride fading.

items.text: Reread: “On a strange and devious way, Siddhartha had gotten into this final and most base of all dependencies, by means of the game of dice.” What does “devious” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?
items.lookFor: devious: indirect and winding; not straightforward.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Devious” here means: indirect and winding; not straightforward. In Sansara, paragraph 6, by a roundabout path, Siddhartha has fallen into his worst dependency, gambling with dice.

items.text: What does “Sansara” suggest about the cycle of desire? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: A stated inference (for example, that desire feeds on itself: each loss makes him want more) backed by one located line, such as the one in Sansara, paragraph 7.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The chapter suggests that desire feeds on itself: each loss makes him want more. Support: “And after each big loss, his mind was set on new riches” (Sansara, paragraph 7).

items.text: Find one example of symbolism in this chapter. What does it reveal that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: Look for objects, places or actions that stand for larger ideas.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The caged songbird (Sansara, paragraphs 10 and 17) stands for the inner voice that has gone silent in him; a plain statement would not carry the sense of beauty kept prisoner and then dead.

items.text: How does the theme in this chapter shape what we understand about the cycle of desire?
items.lookFor: Look for statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The theme of the cycle is named in the game image (“a game which was perhaps enjoyable to play once, twice, ten times—but for ever and ever over again?” (Sansara, paragraph 12)): pleasure repeated endlessly becomes the trap.

items.text: In the passage that begins “She had asked him to tell her about Gotama, and could not hear enough of him, how clear his eyes, how still and beautiful his mouth, how kind his smile, how peaceful his walk had been.”, why might Hesse have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Diction analysis of two words in the anchor passage.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: In Sansara, paragraph 8, “could not hear enough” shows Kamala’s hunger for something her life lacks, and the gentle adjectives “still” and “peaceful” set Gotama’s calm against the restless pleasure-garden; the words quietly prepare her turn toward the Buddha.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Sansara”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: Over many years Siddhartha grows wealthy, gambles, drinks, and becomes greedy and weary—like the childlike people. Kamala tells him she wishes to learn about Gotama. After a dream of Kamala's songbird lying dead in its golden cage, Siddhartha feels disgust at his life and leaves the city without a…
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The cause is the dream of the dead bird and the sadness after it (Sansara, paragraphs 10–11). Effect: he sees that the game is over (paragraph 13) and leaves the city.

items.text: How does “Sansara” build on “With the Childlike People”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal or structural link between this and the previous chapter.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Cause and effect: in “With the Childlike People” he played at trade and love while a quiet voice warned him; here the game takes him over, “For a long time, Siddhartha had lived the life of the world and of lust, though without being a part of it.” (Sansara, paragraph 1)

items.text: What can we infer about a character's motives from what they say and do here, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: An inference about motive supported by a quoted line.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Siddhartha gambles as if he despised money (Sansara, paragraph 7, he “laughed at it”) but dreams of it at night; Kamala claims nothing, but her words about the Buddha (paragraph 8) show she longs for something else too.

items.text: The bell-ringer asked: “What does the dead songbird symbolize?” Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer anchored in the text.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A revised answer should tie the bird to what died in Siddhartha (the inner voice of the previous chapter) and cite “Of this bird he dreamt.” (Sansara, paragraph 10); Kamala freeing it in paragraph 17 adds that she too lets something go.

items.text: Where does tone / mood appear, and how does it connect this chapter to the larger concern with experience versus teaching?
items.lookFor: Look for word choices that reveal the narrator's attitude or the scene's feeling.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The mood is heavy and tired (Sansara, paragraph 5, the veil and the old dress); it connects to the larger concern because despair is what finally turns him back toward the search.

items.text: Background: Samsara (spelled 'Sansara' in this translation) is the cycle of birth, suffering and rebirth. How does knowing this change the way you read one moment in the chapter?
items.lookFor: A specific moment reread in light of the context.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Knowing Samsara is the cycle of birth, suffering and rebirth makes his game image exact (Sansara, paragraph 12): repeated pleasure is itself a small Samsara.

items.text: A critic might argue: “The caged songbird is the book's clearest symbol of Siddhartha's trapped inner voice.” How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the chapter.
items.lookFor: A defended position with evidence and one counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Agree it is a central symbol (paragraphs 10 and 17), but a counterpoint from the text is the old-dress image of paragraph 5 or the game of paragraph 12, which describe the trap just as clearly.

items.text: Which character in this chapter acts most wisely, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: An evaluation using an explicit criterion and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: With self-knowledge as the standard, Kamala is wisest: she frees the bird and keeps her sadness honest (paragraphs 8, 17); Siddhartha least in his gambling (paragraph 6), though he is also the one who finally sees and leaves.

items.text: Rewrite one moment of “Sansara” from the point of view of a different character. What does the new angle reveal or hide about the cycle of desire?
items.lookFor: A rewrite that keeps the chapter’s events accurate, speaks in the chosen character’s voice, and ends with a sentence on what the new angle shows or hides.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Kamala’s view of his disappearance (Sansara, paragraph 17) works well: from her window the departure looks like loss, and it hides the despair under the mango tree.

items.text: Write three questions of your own about “Sansara”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions at three levels, each answerable from the chapter, traded and answered with a line.
followUps: Which of your three questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Example set: recall, ‘What does Kamala do with her bird?’ (paragraph 17); why/how, ‘Why does Siddhartha leave?’ (paragraphs 11–13); what if, ‘Should he have told Kamala?’

items.text: Connect this chapter to the unity of all things: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Hesse need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment of thematic development across the work.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Weak: the chapter shows division, not unity, as he lives without being part of the world (paragraph 1). Hesse would need to show him reconnect with the world, which the river chapters begin.

items.text: Is the symbolism in this chapter effective, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: An evaluative judgment with criteria and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Effective for most readers: the bird is introduced in a dream and paid off by Kamala’s act (paragraph 17). Some find the parallel too neat.

items.text: Compare how “Sansara” treats the cycle of desire with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Siddhartha see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A cross-text synthesis.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A comparison should name a story of success that turns empty and quote “The name of this game was Sansara, a game for children” (Sansara, paragraph 12); Siddhartha’s case is that he knows better and still falls.

items.text: Predict what “By the River” will bring, using two clues from this chapter. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction or judgment justified with textual clues.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Clues: he leaves the city in the night (Sansara, paragraph 16) and remembers his father, Govinda and Gotama (paragraph 14). Prediction: he will return to nature or the river in despair, looking for what he lost.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of this chapter (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about the cycle of desire?
items.lookFor: A modern setting, characters and conflict that keep the chapter’s core idea, with the one element that must not change named.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: A modern version keeps a successful person who wakes up to a life of habits and walks away. What must stay is the moment of seeing the ‘game’ for what it is (paragraph 13).

items.text: What question would you most like to ask Hermann Hesse about this chapter, and what answer do you think the text itself gives?
items.lookFor: A student-generated question answered from evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Example: ‘Why did it take so many years for Siddhartha to leave?’ The text says the tiredness came “slowly, getting a bit denser every day” (Sansara, paragraph 5).

contentNotes.teacherNote: Siddhartha sinks into gambling, drink and self-disgust; be mindful of students affected by addiction in their families. Give the framing announcement before the reading (it covers the first approach to the death wish, paras. 9–13, and the attempt in “By the River”). Brief sexual content: “Never before, it had become so strangely clear to Siddhartha, how closely lust was akin to death.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, Sansara, para. 8)
contentNotes.studentPreview: Siddhartha gambles and drinks and grows to hate his life.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “What has Siddhartha lost, and how does he realize it?”

framing.script: Teacher reads aloud before the reading. Before we read the next chapters, I want to tell you about part of this story. After years of wealth and pleasure, Siddhartha feels empty and disgusted with his life. He leaves the city, and at a river he thinks about ending his life. He doesn't. The sacred word Om comes to him, he sleeps, and he wakes up feeling renewed. Hesse calls the wish an error that Siddhartha wakes up from, and the rest of the book is about finding peace and love. No one in the novel dies by suicide. So let's be clear: if you ever have thoughts of hurting yourself, you deserve support, and help is available. Self-harm is wrong, and it is never the answer to pain; the story shows its cost, not a solution. If you or someone you know is struggling, you can call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org. You can also talk to a school counselor or any trusted adult. You don't have to face it alone.

safeMessaging.teacherScript: Discuss the character's despair and what the text does with it; do not dwell on methods. Before the lesson, remind students that support is available and how to reach the counselor. Check in privately with any student who seems affected and follow your school's referral protocol.
